title: Kiosk Queue Body-Language Lab
oneLiner: A tablet field-test prototype for cafes that logs hesitation, staff rescues, and abandonment at ordering kiosks before complaints pile up.
targetUser: Cafe owners, franchise managers, kiosk vendors, and accessibility auditors observing real customers during slow-hour field tests.
keyUX: Start a test session, run a task script, tap body-language events, mark staff rescue moments, compare completion paths, and export a retrofit priority report.
sourceSignals: S10 - South Korean small merchants rising-cost pressure: https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/2026/06/01/small-business-owners-deepen-pressure-labor-policy-change-and-rising-costs/5611780368680/
stitchPrompt: Create a tablet-friendly responsive web app called "Kiosk Queue Body-Language Lab" for cafe owners, franchise managers, kiosk vendors, and accessibility auditors observing real customers during slow-hour field tests. The app is based on observed user pull: shops already rely on staff rescues, anecdotal complaints, printed menus, and retrofit discussions when customers freeze at kiosks, while small merchants face rising costs and changing retail expectations. The app should use a tablet field-lab mechanic around the trigger moment "the queue freezes at the kiosk or a senior customer complaint arrives" and make the first screen communicate "See where the queue gives up." Use the user's own language: "I need proof of where customers freeze before paying for a retrofit." Build the core workflow around task script, customer profile, kiosk step, hesitation signal, staff assist, abandonment moment, completion time, and retrofit quote, and produce a before/after field report plus retrofit priority list. Required sections: field session header, customer profile and consent-safe notes, task script cards, tap-to-log hesitation grid, staff rescue and abandonment lane, step heatmap, retrofit priority board, and before/after field report. Emotional pressure to make visible: 건강, public embarrassment, accessibility risk, staff interruption, and lost orders. Design direction: use the `field-ops` profile with durable slate/steel tablet panels, large tap-safe controls, restrained cyan action accents, amber friction markers, dense but legible event rows, and no decorative hero. Avoid generic dashboard framing; make the main interaction feel like a real field observer tapping body-language evidence during a live queue.
